evidence_records.Full citation: Zhao, Zhilong, and Yindi Liu. 2025. A Confidence–Diversity Framework for Calibrating AI Judgement in Accessible Qualitative Coding Tasks. arXiv:2508.02029v2.
evidence_records.Title: A Confidence–Diversity Framework for Calibrating AI Judgement in Accessible Qualitative Coding Tasks
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed / peer review not verified
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: confidence/diversity calibration and selective human-review workflow
evidence_records.Research objective: Test whether model self-confidence plus inter-model vote diversity can predict coding agreement and allocate human review in accessible fixed-code tasks.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: deductive qualitative content coding with human–AI adjudication
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Eight LLM variants make 710 binary segment–category judgments, report confidence, and are ensembled; normalized Shannon vote entropy and confidence feed a risk score that routes cases to auto-accept/light/full review, followed by stratified expert audit and six-dataset validation.
evidence_records.Domain: academic-identity interviews plus finance, medicine, law and benchmark text classification
evidence_records.Dataset name: 71 academic-identity interview segments; Finance-News600, PubMed-RCT600, ECHR-A, Moral-Stories, WMT20 QE, XNLI-zh
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: anonymized interview subset and public external datasets released; full identifiable corpus restricted
evidence_records.Number of documents: 71 primary interview segments plus six 600-item/public benchmark subsets
evidence_records.Number of participants: 4 adult interview participants in the primary corpus
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 710 primary segment–code units / 5,680 model decisions; 1,242 audit judgments reported; six external datasets
evidence_records.Document length: short interview segments and benchmark instances
evidence_records.Language: primary corpus not explicitly stated; external set includes English and Chinese
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: identifiable interview corpus restricted under IRB; anonymized replication subset released
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet; GPT-4o and o3-mini; Gemini 2.5 Flash; DeepSeek V3 and Reasoner; release-date labels in paper are not all conventional snapshot IDs
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: single-response and chain-of-thought variants; binary decision plus 1–5 self-confidence; category definition and decision rule; temperature .2/.4
evidence_records.Agent roles: models vote and self-report confidence; risk model routes cases; experts adjudicate selected items
evidence_records.Human role: two research assistants provide baseline; three qualitative researchers blind-code the audit; two senior qualitative scholars adjudicate no-majority cases
evidence_records.Generated outputs: binary codes, confidence, rationales, diversity/risk scores, review tiers and adjudicated labels
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: every request/response logged; labels tie to source segment/category; public raw outputs and prompts
evidence_records.Baselines: two-human coding; confidence-only regression; eight-model majority; alternative weights; six external datasets
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: random seed 42 reported; 10-fold cross-validation and 1,000 bootstrap resamples; one logged response per stated model/configuration
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: accuracy, error rate, Cohen's kappa, Pearson r, R², MAE, normalized Shannon entropy, precision, recall, F1
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: 20% stratified audit by review tier with three blinded researchers and senior adjudication
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two baseline research assistants; three trained qualitative researchers; two senior qualitative-methodology scholars
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: two-human baseline κ=.67; three-researcher audit κ=.82; model majority κ=.89; triaged workflow κ=.93
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: OLS, nested 10-fold CV, Pearson correlation, 1,000-fold bootstrap, two-sided tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction, power analysis
evidence_records.Principal results: Confidence correlated with agreement (r=.82); confidence plus diversity yielded category-level R²=.979. Auto-accept covered 35% with under 5% error and the workflow reported 65% less manual review. External κ gains ranged .20–.78, but tasks were explicitly easy for current LLMs.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: reported 65% reduction in manual review; compute/API cost not reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: SCUT IRB approvals 2024-Q-017/SCUTXWWX230057 and written consent; identifiable corpus restricted; bias, drift and independent audit discussed
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Harvard Dataverse DOI 10.7910/DVN/G1AYGK with prompts, JSON payloads, outputs, scripts, notebooks, figures and anonymized data subset
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: small primary sample, only ten categories, reduced diversity resolution for small panels, accessible-task ceiling effects, no validation on highly interpretive long-context tasks
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Agreement is predicted partly from vote diversity itself and is not interpretive validity; the striking R² uses ten category-level observations, and claims about exceeding human cognition go beyond the accessible-task evidence.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Methodological extension of ensemble uncertainty and selective review to qualitative coding.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Potentially changes the ARR evaluation ranking: include confidence/diversity triage, but require hard-task, held-out and plurality-sensitive validation before treating it as reliable.

evidence_records.Full citation: Xu, Qidi, Nuzha Amjad, Grace Giles, Alexa Cumming, De'angelo Hermesky, Alexander Wen, Min Ji Kwak, and Yejin Kim. 2025. A Multi-Agent Large Language Model Framework for Automated Qualitative Analysis. arXiv:2512.16063v1.
evidence_records.Title: A Multi-Agent Large Language Model Framework for Automated Qualitative Analysis
evidence_records.Authors: Qidi Xu; Nuzha Amjad; Grace Giles; Alexa Cumming; De'angelo Hermesky; Alexander Wen; Min Ji Kwak; Yejin Kim
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed / peer review not verified
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv preprint; no peer-reviewed venue verified in inspected text
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: CoTI system; distinct from other multi-agent thematic-analysis frameworks
evidence_records.Research objective: Automate clue extraction, transcript-level theme generation and cross-transcript codebook development, and test junior-investigator interaction/automation bias.
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: A QwQ-32B Instructor uses four internal roles to refine evidence/reasoning prompts; GPT-4o-mini Thematizer runs three times per transcript and unions outputs; GPT-4o-mini CodebookGenerator clusters themes; outputs are compared to one senior investigator and four junior investigators.
evidence_records.Domain: heart-failure medication experience; external Sierra Leone COVID-19 health-system corpus
evidence_records.Dataset name: 12 heart-failure patient interviews; 21 external COVID-19 interviews
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: heart-failure transcripts restricted; external COVID corpus public
evidence_records.Number of participants: 12 heart-failure patients; four junior-investigator users; external participant count not extracted
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 33 interview transcripts across primary and external checks
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: clinical patient interviews; deidentified and not publicly released
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: objective-specific iterative clue/reasoning prompt optimization; direct-quote constraints; three-run union; interactive retry/feedback UI
evidence_records.Agent roles: Instructor comprises clue, reasoning, evaluation and optimization roles; Thematizer extracts clues/reasoning/themes; CodebookGenerator merges themes
evidence_records.Human role: senior investigator supplies reference analysis; four junior medical investigators manually analyze then use UI; researchers verify prompts, themes and codebook
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: interview, direct-quote clue, theme and cross-interview code
evidence_records.Generated outputs: clues, reasoning chains, themes, structured codebook and user-refined outputs
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: direct quotes are required and retained with themes; codebook contains original themes and representative clues; UI supports source search
evidence_records.Baselines: senior investigator, four junior investigators, QwQ-32B basic LLM, GPT-4o-mini ablations, LDA, Top2Vec and BERTopic
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: three Thematizer runs unioned; one basic-QwQ run; two interviews used for instruction development; no stochastic seeds
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: clue Jaccard/precision/recall/F1; theme/codebook embedding cosine similarity; ablations and response time
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: senior investigator reference; four juniors manually analyze assigned interviews, interact with CoTI, and complete QUEST-informed survey
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: one senior investigator; four medical-school junior investigators; research team
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported; evaluation uses similarity to one senior reference
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive comparisons/ablations; inferential testing not reported
evidence_records.Principal results: CoTI clue Jaccard=.403, precision=.550, recall=.630, F1=.569; theme cosine=.431 and codebook cosine=.621. It beat basic QwQ and topic models, while junior feedback yielded only marginal gains and suggested automation bias.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: about 1 minute/interview for CoTI versus 3 minutes for basic QwQ; about 10 seconds versus 2 minutes for codebook generation
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: UT IRB protocols HSC-MS-21-0874 and HSC-SBMI-13-0549 stated; heart-failure data restricted; participant privacy and conflicts disclosed
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: GitHub https://github.com/QidiXu96/CoTI-MultiAgent-Theme-Analysis; full prompts in supplement; external data at OSF; clinical transcripts unavailable
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: 12-interview single primary case, only four juniors, no senior-feedback condition and limited cross-context validation
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: A single senior analysis is not ground truth; embedding similarity rewards lexical/semantic resemblance rather than interpretive quality, and unioning runs structurally favors recall.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Uses interview data from an earlier clinical study and explicitly compares with TAMA, Auto-TA and Thematic-LM; no duplicate publication detected.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Material RQ1/RQ4/RQ5 evidence: prioritize quote provenance and automation-bias tests; score lower than systems with independent plural human references.

evidence_records.Full citation: Flaherty, Leah Russell, and Kendra H. Oliver. 2025. A Positive Spin: Large Language Models Can Help Directors Evaluate Programs Through Their Patients' Own Words. Pain Reports 10(1):e1219. https://doi.org/10.1097/PR9.0000000000001219.
evidence_records.Title: A Positive Spin: Large Language Models Can Help Directors Evaluate Programs Through Their Patients' Own Words
evidence_records.Authors: Leah Russell Flaherty; Kendra H. Oliver
evidence_records.Publication history notes: received 25 June 2024; accepted 30 October 2024; published online 24 December 2024; 2025 issue/collection; CC BY 4.0
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; full PMC article inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Demonstrate a feasible low-resource LLM-assisted thematic review of pain-program open-ended feedback.
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: All responses are sent once through a staged GPT-4 prompt for detailed open codes and example quotes; one researcher manually reviews/organizes codes into seven themes with model assistance, and two researchers check the final output for fit/hallucination.
evidence_records.Number of documents: 82 responses to one open-ended survey question
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: patient feedback; deidentified before upload and identifying/proprietary details removed
evidence_records.Exact model/version: paid ChatGPT GPT-4; snapshot not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: detailed/open-code instruction, at least five example quotes per code, and repeated request for more codes at least twice
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single chat model plus human review
evidence_records.Agent roles: ChatGPT proposes codes and illustrative quotations
evidence_records.Human role: R1 engineers prompts, manually evaluates codes and organizes themes; R1/R2 review final outputs for thematic fit and hallucination
evidence_records.Generated outputs: at least 15 codes, seven broad themes and supporting quotations
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: the prompt requires five exact sample quotes per code; full exchange and supplement are linked
evidence_records.Baselines: no independent human-only or model baseline
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one chat workflow with at least two follow-up generations; no independent replicate
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: two authors manually checked all reported codes/themes and quotes; no blinded or independent evaluation
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two authors, including pain-program and responsible-data-science expertise
evidence_records.Principal results: Seven themes were produced; manual review found four example quotes that did not clearly fit their assigned theme but no fabricated quotes.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: described as ergonomic/time-saving; no measured time or cost
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Allegheny Singer Research Institute designated project 2022-239 QA/QI; deidentification and cloud-data/privacy risks are explicitly discussed
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: full shared ChatGPT exchange and supplementary theme table; raw patient responses not released; model snapshot absent
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: LLMs tend toward description rather than interpretation, are opaque, require validation and prompt skill, and can create privacy risks
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: No human-only comparator, no repeated runs, no reliability metric and author-only checking; claims about bias mitigation or unexpected insight are not causally established.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Applied program-evaluation use case rather than a system benchmark.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Low-ranked evidence for performance but strong illustrative case for quote verification, disclosure, privacy, and separating speed claims from validity.

evidence_records.Full citation: Yue, Yongjie, Dong Liu, Yilin Lv, Junyi Hao, and Peixuan Cui. 2025. A Practical Guide and Assessment on Using ChatGPT to Conduct Grounded Theory: Tutorial. Journal of Medical Internet Research 27:e70122. https://doi.org/10.2196/70122.
evidence_records.Title: A Practical Guide and Assessment on Using ChatGPT to Conduct Grounded Theory: Tutorial
evidence_records.Authors: Yongjie Yue; Dong Liu; Yilin Lv; Junyi Hao; Peixuan Cui
evidence_records.Publication history notes: received 16 December 2024; accepted 15 April 2025; published 14 May 2025; CC BY
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; full PMC article and appendices inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Provide a reproducible three-stage ChatGPT grounded-theory tutorial and compare its coding with independent NVivo-assisted manual analysis.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: grounded theory: open, axial and selective coding
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Two researchers manually code in NVivo; a separate researcher feeds eight Chinese transcripts to ChatGPT 4-Turbo in chunks and iteratively requests open, clustered/axial and selective codes, with manual screening/refinement; an expert plus two researchers semantically align outputs before computing agreement.
evidence_records.Domain: blind gamers' experiences in a Chinese MMORPG
evidence_records.Dataset name: Listen and Play in Jianghu interview corpus
evidence_records.Document length: semi-structured interviews; some split because of context limits
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: interviews with blind participants; anonymized and ethics-approved
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT 4-Turbo; snapshot not reported; paper states an 8,192-token context
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: role prompt, iterative open coding with source alignment, repeated depth requests, paired-transcript axial clustering, and selective-code relationship prompts
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single model with extensive human iteration
evidence_records.Agent roles: ChatGPT proposes codes, clusters/categories, core category and theory relationships
evidence_records.Human role: two independent manual coders create comparison analysis; another researcher operates ChatGPT; one expert and two researchers semantically align codes; humans refine every AI stage and return to source interviews
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: text segment, open-code node/reference point, axial category and selective/core category
evidence_records.Generated outputs: 274 open codes, seven main categories, a core category and preliminary theoretical framework
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: open-code prompts require exact source statements; appendices provide full coding outputs, theory diagrams and generic prompts
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: repeated conversational queries but no independent stochastic replications
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: node/reference/coverage counts, percent agreement, Cohen's kappa distributions and t tests
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: one domain expert and two researchers inspect semantic equivalence of 274 AI and 289 manual open codes and compare axial/selective relationships
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two manual researchers, one ChatGPT-operating researcher, one domain expert and two semantic-alignment reviewers, with some role overlap
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: manual coders reached more than 85% before full coding; raw human–AI agreement exceeded 95% largely because most text was uncoded, while the largest κ category was only slight agreement
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: SPSS t tests for node/reference/coverage differences; descriptive κ distributions
evidence_records.Principal results: Manual and AI counts did not significantly differ, but ChatGPT had weaker depth, context, connection and organization. Manual analysis made eight categories versus seven AI categories; core narratives overlapped after human reconstruction.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: manual NVivo analysis took three weeks for two researchers; ChatGPT analysis took one day after prompts were finalized
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Renmin University ethics approval 20220028; informed consent, withdrawal right, anonymization and 50 RMB compensation; privacy/bias risks discussed
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: OA full article; appendices contain workflows, complete coding results, theory and prompts; interview corpus not released and model snapshot absent
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: eight participants, one Chinese context, one model, instability/bias and need for multi-model/longitudinal replication
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Semantic alignment was performed before agreement computation and high raw agreement was inflated by uncoded text; grounded theory relies heavily on human screening/reconstruction, so the study does not show autonomous theory generation.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Empirical tutorial extending earlier ChatGPT thematic/grounded-theory case studies.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Material RQ2/RQ5 evidence for explicit claimed-versus-operationalized coding, source-linked comparisons, manual reconstruction and prevalence-aware agreement reporting.

evidence_records.Full citation: Ahtisham, Bakhtawar, Kirk Vanacore, Jinsook Lee, Zhuqian Zhou, Doug Pietrzak, and Rene F. Kizilcec. 2026. AI Annotation Orchestration: Evaluating LLM Verifiers to Improve the Quality of LLM Annotations in Learning Analytics. LAK 2026. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785022.3785095.
evidence_records.Title: AI Annotation Orchestration: Evaluating LLM Verifiers to Improve the Quality of LLM Annotations in Learning Analytics
evidence_records.Authors: Bakhtawar Ahtisham; Kirk Vanacore; Jinsook Lee; Zhuqian Zhou; Doug Pietrzak; Rene F. Kizilcec
evidence_records.Venue: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026)
evidence_records.Publication history notes: screened from 2025 arXiv:2511.09785v2; inspected text is the LAK 2026 proceedings version with DOI and April–May 2026 venue dates
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv-hosted proceedings text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: 2025 preprint / 2026 peer-reviewed version family; verifier-orchestration study
evidence_records.Research objective: Compare unverified, self-verified and every directional cross-verified combination of three LLMs for qualitative tutoring-move annotation.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive–deductive qualitative codebook development followed by deductive tutor-move coding
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: A human develops/refines an 11-class single-best-fit rubric; author–Gemini agreement plus blinded human adjudication creates the reference; GPT-5, Claude 3 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Flash annotate each tutor utterance, then self- or cross-verify against the same rubric.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid codebook development, then deductive coding
evidence_records.Document length: session chunks with median about 80 turns and 1–2-turn overlap
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-5; Claude 3 Sonnet; Gemini 2.5 Flash; provider snapshot IDs not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: same rubric-grounded prompt with definitions/concise examples; focal tutor utterance plus preceding student and prior tutor turn; verifier sees initial label/rationale and retains or revises
evidence_records.Agent roles: base model assigns one move and rationale; same/different model audits against rubric
evidence_records.Human role: Author 1 manually codes and builds codebook; external experienced tutoring reviewer blindly adjudicates author–Gemini disagreements; humans remain proposed edge-case adjudicators
evidence_records.Generated outputs: single tutor-move label, rationale, verification decision and final label
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: logs initial label, verification decision, final label and rubric-grounded justification; source turn context retained
evidence_records.Baselines: three unverified models; self-verification; all six directional cross-verifier pairs; human–Gemini adjudicated reference
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one pass per orchestration configuration; no stochastic replication/seeds reported
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: blinded disagreement-focused external adjudication of 501 human–Gemini disagreements
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: one author coder/codebook developer and one external reviewer experienced in human tutoring implementation/research
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: unverified mean κ=.32; self-verification mean .64; cross-verification mean .44; verified overall mean .51
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive per-construct/per-pair kappa comparisons; no uncertainty intervals/significance tests reported
evidence_records.Principal results: Self-verification almost doubled mean κ and improved every model; cross-verification averaged +37% but was directional and sometimes harmful. Intent-heavy Prompting/Revoicing remained hard.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: described as scalable/low-cost but compute cost and latency were not optimized or reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: data are described as deidentified/pseudonymized; IRB, consent, access and fairness analysis are not reported in the inspected paper
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: full rubric reportedly in supplements; no verified public data/code/prompts repository or provider snapshot IDs
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: 30 sessions, one math domain, text-only, one rubric/prompt family, single-label assumption, model updates and unmeasured compute/latency
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Reference labels partly inherit Gemini: all human–Gemini agreements are accepted and only disagreements are independently reviewed, creating possible correlated-model bias; no repeated runs establish stability.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: The 2025 arXiv record and 2026 LAK DOI are one version family and must be counted once.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Material RQ3/RQ5 evidence: self-verification rises in ranking, but cross-verifier direction must be tuned and a fully independent human reference remains mandatory.

evidence_records.Full citation: Flanders, Samuel, Melati Nungsari, and Mark Cheong Wing Loong. 2025. AI Coding with Few-Shot Prompting for Thematic Analysis. arXiv:2504.07408v1.
evidence_records.Title: AI Coding with Few-Shot Prompting for Thematic Analysis
evidence_records.Authors: Samuel Flanders; Melati Nungsari; Mark Cheong Wing Loong
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed / peer review not verified
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv PDF inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Improve passage-level AI thematic codes with error-driven prompt iteration and semantically matched few-shot examples.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: coding for thematic analysis in a coding-reliability/positivist framing
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: GPT-3.5 Turbo summarizes 2,530 news articles and labels passages; Ada embeddings, UMAP/HDBSCAN and later k-means form semantic clusters; a long Socratic pipeline generates cluster exemplars; final few-shot prompts code theme, speaker/target and valence; three reviewers iteratively validate a fixed sample.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: LLM-inductive exemplar/code generation followed by prompt-guided passage coding
evidence_records.Dataset name: 2,530 Malaysian news articles from five outlets, 2017–2023
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: source articles public; compiled corpus/review sheets not clearly archived at a working URL
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 2,530 articles segmented at line breaks; 414 passages in fixed human-review sample
evidence_records.Document length: articles summarized; passages shorter than 50 characters initially dropped and stricter length filters added later
evidence_records.Language: English-language Malaysian news (paper does not fully characterize multilingual coverage)
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public news about refugees, a vulnerable population; representational risks discussed only indirectly
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-3.5-Turbo and Ada embedding model; snapshot IDs not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: initial concise theme prompt; error-driven Socratic relevance/context/valence steps; JSON outputs; semantically matched cluster-code summaries as few-shot exemplars
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no weight tuning; prompts revised using human-review errors
evidence_records.Agent roles: GPT summarizes, codes and produces exemplar themes; embeddings/clustering retrieve examples
evidence_records.Human role: three reviewers independently rate codes, keep diaries, discuss disagreements, define error modes, revise the workflow and establish consensus reference labels
evidence_records.Generated outputs: relevance decision, specific theme, attitude holder, target and hostile/sympathetic valence
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: review sheets include article URL/full text/title/summary/passage/code/cluster; final prompts retain the focal passage and matched examples
evidence_records.Baselines: initial one-pass prompt versus final Socratic/few-shot workflow; no independent non-LLM model baseline
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: two evaluated workflow iterations on the same 414-passage sample; no stochastic seeds
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, negative predictive value, Kendall's tau-b and exact confidence intervals
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: three independent reviewers assess a fixed 414-passage sample, discuss disagreements and produce consensus; 153 model-irrelevant passages receive additional review
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: three human reviewers; domain/method expertise not fully specified
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: final Kendall tau-b all items: .950/.780/.763 by pair; among model-coded-relevant items: .917/.519/.473
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: Clopper–Pearson 95% intervals and pairwise Kendall tau-b with p-values
evidence_records.Principal results: Initial precision=.496. Final accuracy=.812, precision=.719, recall=.974, F1=.825 and NPV=.968. Strong performance mostly reflects relevance filtering; about 30% of generated codes lacked consensus support.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: pipeline is designed to use cheap GPT-3.5 and concise examples; authors acknowledge substantial reviewer/prompt-development labor and do not give total cost/time
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: no formal ethics statement; vulnerable-group representation, scraping rights and bias governance are not systematically addressed
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: complete prompt text and extensive appendix examples/communications; referenced coding-document URL is unresolved in the inspected PDF; no verified code/data package
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: summary bleeding, passage ambiguity, general inaccuracy, model limits, human uncertainty and heavy iterative reviewer work
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The fixed sample informed workflow redesign and final evaluation, so estimates are development-set rather than held-out performance; consensus discussions also change the human reference.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Builds on Dai, Morgan and De Paoli; not a duplicate of other retrieved records.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Material RQ3/RQ5 evidence for semantically matched examples and error logs, but ARR should penalize no held-out test, heavy hidden human labor and relevance-dominated metrics.

evidence_records.Full citation: Sulaiman, Muhammad Hafiz, Nora Muda, and Fatimah Abdul Razak. 2025. Analyzing Patient Complaints in Web-Based Reviews of Private Hospitals in Selangor, Malaysia, Using Large Language Model–Assisted Content Analysis: Mixed Methods Study. JMIR Formative Research 9:e69075. https://doi.org/10.2196/69075.
evidence_records.Title: Analyzing Patient Complaints in Web-Based Reviews of Private Hospitals in Selangor, Malaysia, Using Large Language Model–Assisted Content Analysis: Mixed Methods Study
evidence_records.Authors: Muhammad Hafiz Sulaiman; Nora Muda; Fatimah Abdul Razak
evidence_records.Publication history notes: received 21 November 2024; accepted 7 April 2025; published 27 June 2025; CC BY
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; full PMC article/appendices inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Develop and validate a scalable LLM-assisted hospital-review coding pipeline and derive interpretable issue factors.
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Reviews are scraped, fake/positive/no-issue records filtered, GPT-4o-mini induces a 41-code codebook from 200 extracts over five iterations, a health-management team reviews it, one human and GPT apply 0–4 severity codes to 200 reviews, GPT codes the remainder, and factor analysis reduces codes to six themes.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: inductive LLM codebook then deductive severity coding and factor analysis
evidence_records.Domain: private-hospital patient complaints in Selangor, Malaysia
evidence_records.Dataset name: 2023 web-based reviews for all 53 Selangor private hospitals
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: public source reviews; processed LACA data restricted because hospital/doctor names may remain
evidence_records.Number of documents: 14,938 reviews collected; 12,035 had comments; 1,279 issue reviews analyzed
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 14,938 reviews; 200 for code induction and 200 for human–GPT validation; 41 codes
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public health-care complaints can identify hospitals/doctors; final visualizations deidentified and full LACA data restricted
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4o mini API; snapshot/settings not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: issue yes/no filtering, five iterative codebook generations, then per-code 0–4 severity labeling; full prompts in appendices
evidence_records.Agent roles: GPT filters issues, induces codes/definitions and applies severity labels
evidence_records.Human role: health-care management experts review final code list; one human coder labels the 200-review validation sample; researchers interpret factor labels
evidence_records.Generated outputs: 41-code codebook, per-review severity matrix and six latent issue factors
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: sample source comments and code assignments are published; factor-analysis dataset released; full source-to-code matrix restricted
evidence_records.Baselines: one human coder for 200 reviews; global literature patterns as informal external comparison
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: five codebook-induction iterations; no repeated final coding/seeds
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen's kappa, factor loadings/eigenvalues, cumulative explained variance and Cronbach alpha
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: one human independently applies every code to 200 random reviews; health-management experts inspect codebook
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: one human coder plus health-care management experts; exact count/independence not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: human–GPT per-document κ ranged .44–1.00; reported mean .81
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: factor analysis; six factors explain .74 cumulative variance; alpha .88–.97 except Patient Rights/Accessibility .61
evidence_records.Principal results: GPT induced 41 partly overlapping/nongranular codes. Six factors were interpreted; authors report mean κ=.81, though their unusual averaging unit and binarization need caution.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: claimed cost-effective and real-time capable; actual time/API cost not reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: public secondary data judged exempt under Malaysian MREC guidance; identifiers removed from results, access restricted and authorized processing described
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: OA article, seven multimedia appendices with prompts/codebook/sample outputs, and factor-analysis data on Google Drive; sensitive LACA matrix available on request
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: web-review selection/information bias, one geography/private sector, platform/user differences and nongranular codes
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The paper argues the model must understand overlapping codes because alpha is high, which does not follow; one human and average per-document binary κ do not establish interpretive validity, and factor analysis transforms rather than validates themes.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Applied extension of Chew et al.'s LACA framework.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Material claimed-versus-operationalized example: ARR should require code-granularity audit, standard reliability units, independent codebook review and prohibit latent-factor consistency from standing in for qualitative validity.

evidence_records.Full citation: Hila, Angjelin, and Elliott Hauser. 2025. Assessing the Reliability of Large Language Models for Deductive Qualitative Coding: A Comparative Study of ChatGPT Interventions. arXiv:2507.14384v1.
evidence_records.Title: Assessing the Reliability of Large Language Models for Deductive Qualitative Coding: A Comparative Study of ChatGPT Interventions
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed / peer review not verified
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv PDF inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Measure ChatGPT deductive coding reliability and compare zero-shot, few-shot, definition and step-by-step interventions with supervised models.
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: ChatGPT classifies public U.S. Supreme Court summaries into a fixed 21-major/220-subtopic CAP taxonomy; four prompt interventions are tested in 30 stratified 50-case samples after extensive full-dataset prompt optimization, with BiLSTM and RoBERTa baselines.
evidence_records.Dataset name: Comparative Agendas Project Supreme Court Cases dataset
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 9,330 summaries with 21 major topics and up to 220 subtopics; evaluation uses 30×50 stratified cases per intervention
evidence_records.Document length: case summaries of at least two sentences
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT-4o, 4.5, o1 and o1-mini used across interactive work; allocation by test not fully specified; custom RoBERTa/BiLSTM
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: zero-shot class names; labeled few-shot examples; formal definitions/keywords; case-by-case step-by-step evidence and rationale; iterative feedback on ground truth during development
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: BiLSTM/RoBERTa trained on same dataset; ChatGPT not weight-tuned but prompts optimized over a full classification epoch
evidence_records.Agent roles: ChatGPT assigns label and reasoning; supervised baselines assign labels
evidence_records.Human role: CAP human labels/codebook are treated as reference; authors engineer and revise prompts/error heuristics; no new independent human evaluation
evidence_records.Generated outputs: major policy label, sublabel and step-by-step justification
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: interactive prompt links evidence/rationale to final label; public case summaries and CAP labels are available
evidence_records.Baselines: unassisted ChatGPT, BiLSTM and RoBERTa; four prompt interventions
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: 30 stratified samples of 50 for each intervention; separate chats; no API seed/snapshot control
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, macro/weighted F1, Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff alpha, Spearman rho, chi-square, Cramér's V
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: no new human evaluation; uses existing CAP labels as ground truth
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: CAP coders not described in this paper; authors perform method development
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: step-by-step κ=.744 and α=.746; baseline ChatGPT major κ=.46; RoBERTa major κ=.75
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: within-/between-method chi-square tests, Bonferroni/FDR correction and Cramér's V
evidence_records.Principal results: Step-by-step accuracy=.775, weighted F1=.755, κ=.744, nearly matching RoBERTa accuracy/F1=.79 and κ=.75. Models degraded around the 30th–40th summary and struggled with broad overlapping classes.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: scalability discussed; computational/time cost not quantified and interactive strategy is more expensive
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: public legal dataset; no human-subject ethics issue, but no broader bias/responsible-use audit
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: CAP data/codebook public and prompts/flowcharts shown; no verified code/output repository, exact model allocation or seed
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: CAP label validity not independently verified, codebook/category ambiguity, model/prompt variance and input-length/complexity confounds
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Prompt optimization used ground truth across a full epoch before evaluation, so leakage/overfitting is possible; the task is conventional fixed-label classification and offers limited evidence about interpretive qualitative analysis.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Extends prior CAP/nCoder/ChatGPT fixed-code comparisons; no duplicate version found.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Material RQ3/RQ5 baseline for step decomposition and supervised comparisons, but ARR should rank it below held-out, independently human-evaluated qualitative studies.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Adequate for the stated claim: accuracy, precision, recall, macro/weighted F1, Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff alpha, Spearman rho, chi-square, Cramér's V; Prompt optimization used ground truth across a full epoch before evaluation, so leakage/overfitting is possible; the task is conventional fixed-label classification and offers limited evidence about interpretive qualitative analysis.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Absent or inadequate for the stated claim: CAP human labels/codebook are treated as reference; authors engineer and revise prompts/error heuristics; no new independent human evaluation; Prompt optimization used ground truth across a full epoch before evaluation, so leakage/overfitting is possible; the task is conventional fixed-label classification and offers limited evidence about interpretive qualitative analysis.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Adequate for the stated claim: interactive prompt links evidence/rationale to final label; public case summaries and CAP labels are available

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Adequate for the stated claim: 30 stratified samples of 50 for each intervention; separate chats; no API seed/snapshot control

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: Partial/claim-limited: public legal dataset; no human-subject ethics issue, but no broader bias/responsible-use audit

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Partial/claim-limited: CAP data/codebook public and prompts/flowcharts shown; no verified code/output repository, exact model allocation or seed; ChatGPT-4o, 4.5, o1 and o1-mini used across interactive work; allocation by test not fully specified; custom RoBERTa/BiLSTM

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Partial/claim-limited: CAP label validity not independently verified, codebook/category ambiguity, model/prompt variance and input-length/complexity confounds; Prompt optimization used ground truth across a full epoch before evaluation, so leakage/overfitting is possible; the task is conventional fixed-label classification and offers limited evidence about interpretive qualitative analysis.
